newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN envoy calls for step-by-step Cyprus talks.
newsitem.headline: UN envoy calls for step-by-step Cyprus talks.

text.p: Talks aimed at reuniting Cyprus began on Monday with the U.N. special envoy for the divided island urging the Greek and Turkish Cypriot rivals to go step by step rather than take an all-or-nothing approach.

Diego Cordovez said he did not expect the decades-old problem to be solved at the five-day meeting between Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash at a luxury hotel overlooking Lake Geneva in the village of Glion near Montreux.

"It will be different. We are changing the procedure. It has to be an incremental thing where you go slowly building an agreement," Cordovez told reporters at the hotel, where he is chairing the U.N.-brokered talks under a media blackout.

"If we continue to work with the sense that we are involved in a process you cannot solve the Cyprus problem in four days which is what they did every time. I am not expecting them to solve the problems now," Cordovez added.
"In the past, they started from zero and ended with zero. They started from zero trying to get one hundred."

Diplomats say this approach would be more in tune with the Levantine aspect of the east Mediterranean island where things tend to move slowly, despite international pressure for a quick solution -- and would help the mediators to dampen expectations.
Earlier, Denktash and Clerides put on a display of joviality as they met for the formal opening of the talks, the second round since a first meeting in Troutbeck, New York, last month.
But diplomats analysing comments made by both sides in advance of the talks and the current situation on the island said prospects for movement towards a solution looked dim.
Clerides and Denktash, clad in dark suits, appeared relaxed and joked with each other and complimented the hotel cuisine as reporters looked on as they and their teams sat down for the discussions.
Around the green-baize table with them was Cordovez, a former foreign minister of Ecuador.
Neither spoke to reporters but Denktash adviser Ergun Olgun told Reuters: "We're here to keep the talks going."

Gloom was deepened in advance of the meeting by Denktash who, after arriving in Switzerland on Sunday, insisted on absolute political equality with the 78-year-old Clerides -- anathema to the Greek Cypriots.
"There really seems little chance of any sort of breakthrough," said one envoy close to the talks, being held amid high security.

The 73-year-old Denktash, head of the breakaway northern Turkish Cypriot administration recognised only by Turkey, told Reuters in an interview on Sunday the talks could proceed only on the basis of political equality on paper and in effect.

"The attempt to set up a federal partnership failed so far because a federal partnership can only be established between two equals. That equality has been destroyed by the world by treating the Greek Cypriot partner as the government of all," Denktash said.

Public positions have become more entrenched since Troutbeck. Stakes are also higher as Cyprus prepares for entry talks with the European Union next year and Turkey says it will move towards partial integration with the north.

Denktash accused the EU of getting in the way of a deal and threatened to pull out of the negotiations: "If the EU talks start, the intercommunal talks will stop and that will be the end of the matter," he said.
Cordovez said there would be a give-and-take between the two sides but one at a time. He did not say how his new approach would fit in with the EU timetable for entry talks for Cyprus.
Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both communities broke apart amid violence.
They have been separated since 1974 when Turkey invaded the northern third of the island in response to a coup in the capital Nicosia, backed by the junta then ruling Greece.
